segments.text: Territorial sovereignty is the state’s legal authority over its territory, subject to international obligations.
Prepare acquisition and loss of territory in classical doctrine, boundaries, land territory, internal waters/territorial sea and the idea that sovereignty entails both rights and duties.

Territorial sovereignty means that a state possesses primary legal authority over its territory while remaining bound by international law. Sovereignty therefore combines competence with obligation. A state may control entry, regulate persons and property, and administer public authority within its territory, but it must also respect treaty duties, immunities, human rights obligations and the sovereign rights of other states.

Territorial title and territorial administration are related but distinct. A state may claim legal title while another entity exercises practical control, and disputes may require examination of treaties, historical title, conduct, boundary instruments and effectivités.

Classical doctrine discussed occupation, cession, prescription, conquest and accretion, but modern international law—especially the prohibition on acquisition of territory by unlawful force—changes how historical categories can be used. A contemporary answer should not reproduce nineteenth-century modes without explaining modern legal constraints.

Land territory should be distinguished from maritime zones. Internal waters and the territorial sea are closely connected to sovereignty, while the exclusive economic zone and continental shelf involve sovereign rights for specified purposes rather than full territorial sovereignty. Airspace above land territory and territorial sea is also part of the territorial legal framework.

International law places strong value on boundary stability. Treaty boundaries and inherited administrative boundaries can have enduring legal effect, and boundary arrangements are often treated differently from ordinary treaty obligations because stability of territory is central to international order.

items.text: Territorial sovereignty means a state has primary legal authority over its land territory and related maritime and air spaces, but that authority operates subject to international obligations.
Territorial questions can involve title, boundaries, administration, treaties and effective exercise of authority. Historical possession alone may not settle a modern legal dispute.

Land territory should be studied together with internal waters, territorial sea and airspace at a basic conceptual level. Different maritime zones carry different legal rights, so avoid using “territory” loosely for every sea area.
Sovereignty includes duties as well as rights, including respect for treaty obligations and the rights of other states under international law.

rows: Common confusion to avoid: Do not describe sovereignty as unlimited freedom. International legal obligations are constraints that a sovereign state itself is required to respect.

items.text: Map land, sea and air dimensions.
Study boundary disputes through title, effectivités and treaty interpretation at a basic level.

segments.text: Territory is a foundation of state authority.
Sovereignty is not unlimited; treaties and customary law constrain its exercise.
